lesson.title: be- & er- Verb Factory
lesson.subtitle: bekommen, erinnern, erklären — meaning-shapers, and stress as the test

hook.title: The Meaning-Shapers
hook.content: ver- is the cognate star, but be- and er- are the factory workers. be- converts: bekommen (come by → GET), besuchen (seek → VISIT), bestellen (order — place-at!). er- achieves: erinnern (inner-ize → REMEMBER), erklären (clear-out → EXPLAIN), erkennen (know-out → RECOGNIZE), erledigen? hint — (done-out → finish). English once ran the same factory — be-think (bethought), be-come, and the archaic 'I would bethink me' — but retired it. The stress test tells you which factory a verb comes from: inseparable prefixes never take the stress, separable prefixes always do. Stress is the separable-detector.

footnotes.title: The Stress Detector
footnotes.content: Say them: AUFwachen (separable — stress on the prefix) vs verSTEHen (inseparable — stress on the root). beKOMmen, erKLÄren — unstressed prefix. The rule: if the prefix is stressed, it will fly to the sentence end; if not, it stays welded. Hear the stress, know the grammar.

pattern.title: The Factory Floor
pattern.content: The be- floor: bekommen (GET — the trap!), besuchen (visit), bestellen (order), bezahlen (pay — the 'by-tally'! zahlen = pay/count), beginnen (begin — the same word as begin!). The er- floor: erinnern (remember), erklären (explain), erkennen (recognize), erledigen (finish off — hint), erreichen (reach — erreichen/er- + reichen, to reach!). Both factories take ge--free participles: bekommen, besucht, erinnert, erklärt. And the productive test: meet a new verb with be-/er-/ver- and you know — inseparable, ge--free, root-stressed, and the prefix is doing meaning-work.
pattern.linguist_note: beginnen and English begin are twins (both *biginnan, 'to open/undertake') — be- in both! The factory is older than the languages' split: be- and er- (Germanic *uz-, cognate with Latin ex-) were prefix-verbs in Proto-Germanic itself.

exercises.prompt: The factory floor — match each verb with its product:
exercises.meaning: to visit, to recognize, to remember, to explain, to pay
exercises.explanation: be- converts, er- achieves — and each product is ge--free in the participle: besucht, erkannt, erinnert, erklärt, bezahlt.

exercises.prompt: The stress test: which verb is SEPARABLE (stressed prefix)?
exercises.meaning: Stressed prefix = separable = it will fly
exercises.explanation: auf- takes the stress and the flight; ver-/be-/er- stay unstressed and welded. Hear the stress, predict the grammar. The separable shelf — einkaufen, abfahren — flies its prefixes; verdienen welds ver- like the rest of the factory.
Inseparable prefix blocks ge-: erklärt, bekommen, verstanden — the No-ge- Club's third wing.

exercises.prompt: What English verb is the true twin of 'beginnen'?
exercises.explanation: Both *biginnan: the be- prefix is Germanic heritage, not a German invention — English's begin kept it too.

exercises.prompt: Assemble: 'He explains the word and I remember it'
exercises.target_answer: Er erklärt das Wort und ich erinnere mich
exercises.meaning: He explains the word and I remember it

vocab_hints.note: sich erinnern — remember is reflexive in German: 'inner-ize MYSELF'

exercises.explanation: Two er- factory verbs in one sentence — and erinnern demands its reflexive mich: the inner-izing needs a target.

summary.outcome: Use be-/er- verbs with ge--free participles and apply the stress test to new verbs.

use_example.german: Er erklärt das Wort und ich erinnere mich.
use_example.english: He explains the word and I remember it.

summary.takeaway: be- converts, er- achieves — both factories are unstressed, ge--free, and detectable by stress alone.
summary.curiosity_teaser: Next: sich & the lost reflexives — hie thee hence: the pronouns English dropped, the daily verbs that kept them.

twist.prompt: Without looking back — rebuild the core sentence from be- & er- Verb Factory (He explains the word and I remember it):
twist.target_answer: Er erklärt das Wort und ich erinnere mich
twist.explanation: Re-assembling "Er erklärt das Wort und ich erinnere mich" from scratch locks in the structural pattern of be- & er- Verb Factory without relying on short-term echo.

bekommen.etymology_derivation: be- (by/around) + kommen (come) — literally 'come by (something)'; English become is the same be + come with a different job. [wiktionary]

erinnern.etymology_derivation: er- (out/thorough) + innern (inner) — to 'internal-ize' a thing; built on inn(inner), the twin of English inner. [wiktionary]

erklären.etymology_derivation: er- (out) + klar (clear) — 'to make clear'; klar and clear are both medieval loans of Latin clarus. [wiktionary]

verstehen.etymology_derivation: Inseparable: ver- (for-) + stehen (stand). Past participle: verstanden (no ge-).

versuchen.context_translation: I am trying to find it.

beginnen.context_phrase: Der Film beginnt um acht Uhr.
beginnen.context_translation: The film begins at eight o'clock.
beginnen.etymology_derivation: From Proto-Germanic *biginnaną; the page documents cognate English begin — an exact class 3 ablaut twin: began and begann, begun and begonnen. [wiktionary]

bezahlen.etymology_derivation: be- + zahlen — the inseparable prefix at work on the tale-family verb. [wiktionary]

einkaufen.etymology_derivation: ein (in) + kaufen (to buy) — buy in, do the shopping; the kaufen root is the German twin of English cheap. [wiktionary]

abfahren.etymology_derivation: ab (off) + fahren (to drive): to drive off — the same verb root as English fare. [wiktionary]

verdienen.context_translation: She earns a lot of money.
verdienen.etymology_derivation: From ver- + dienen (to serve), a calque of Latin deservio - the same Latin verb that gave English deserve (via Old French deservir). [wiktionary][etymonline]

hart.context_phrase: Das Brot ist heute sehr hart.
hart.context_translation: The bread is very hard today.
hart.etymology_derivation: From Old High German hart, Proto-Germanic *harduz, the exact twin of English hard; both trace to the same Indo-European root meaning strong. [wiktionary]

unwetter.context_phrase: Bei dem Unwetter bleibt das Flugzeug am Boden.
unwetter.context_translation: During the storm the plane stays on the ground.
unwetter.etymology_derivation: Un- (bad) plus Wetter (weather — twin of English weather); literally un-weather, severe weather. The page even names the fossil English twin unweather. [wiktionary]

alles.etymology_derivation: Old High German allaz, the neuter of all 'all' + -es: literally all of it. [wiktionary]

post.context_phrase: Ich bringe das Paket zur Post.
post.context_translation: I am taking the package to the post office.
post.etymology_derivation: Borrowed from Italian posta, the relay-station word from Latin positus (placed) — the same post English uses for mail; German kept a pf-twin, Pfosten. [wiktionary]

gefahr.context_translation: Be careful, there is danger here.
gefahr.etymology_derivation: From Proto-Germanic *fērō (danger); the page documents cognate English fear — fear began as the danger itself. [wiktionary]

th_to_d.name: The Dental Shift (TH → D)
th_to_d.historical_linguistics: Every single original Germanic "th" sound systematically shifted to "d" in High German, while English kept the ancient "th".
th_to_d.philological_note: Around 500–700 AD in the High German Consonant Shift, dental fricatives hardened into voiced dental stops.

d_to_t.name: The Stop Shift (D → T)
d_to_t.historical_linguistics: Where English kept Germanic "d", High German hardened it into "t".
d_to_t.philological_note: Voiced stops became voiceless. Explains pairs like day ↔ Tag, door ↔ Tür, and drink ↔ trinken.
d_to_t.literature_source: Complementary to the TH → D shift: as TH took over D, original D shifted to T in High German.

p_to_pf_f.name: The Labial Shift (P → PF / F)
p_to_pf_f.historical_linguistics: Proto-Germanic /p/ shifted to the affricate "pf" at the beginning of words, and to "f" or "ff" after vowels.
p_to_pf_f.philological_note: Explains apple ↔ Apfel, pepper ↔ Pfeffer, hope ↔ hoffen, and sleep ↔ schlafen.

t_to_s_ss_z.name: The Sibilant Shift (T → S / SS / Z)
t_to_s_ss_z.historical_linguistics: Proto-Germanic /t/ shifted to sibilant "s/ss/ß" after vowels, and to "z" (/ts/) at the beginning of words.
t_to_s_ss_z.philological_note: Reveals water ↔ Wasser, eat ↔ essen, better ↔ besser, two ↔ zwei, and to ↔ zu.
t_to_s_ss_z.literature_source: Walter Skeat - Primary dental affrication and spirantization

k_to_ch.name: The Velar Shift (K → CH)
k_to_ch.historical_linguistics: Proto-Germanic /k/ softened to the fricative "ch" in medial and final positions.
k_to_ch.philological_note: The Ach-Laut [x] occurs after a, o, u; the Ich-Laut [ç] occurs after e, i, ä, ö, ü.

v_to_b.name: The Bilabial Shift (V / F → B)
v_to_b.historical_linguistics: Intervocalic /v/ and /f/ in English regularly correspond to voiced /b/ in German.
v_to_b.philological_note: Explains give ↔ geben, live ↔ leben, love ↔ lieben, over ↔ über, and seven ↔ sieben.
v_to_b.literature_source: Proto-Germanic bilabial spirant closing to stop in High German

y_gh_to_g_ch.name: The Palatal & Guttural Link (Y → G & GH → CH)
y_gh_to_g_ch.historical_linguistics: English vocalized palatal "g" into "y" (say, day, yesterday) and silenced "gh" (night, laugh, light). German preserved them as "g" or "ch".
y_gh_to_g_ch.philological_note: Explains why English spelling has silent 'gh' letters — they were original German-like gutturals!

latin_ieren.name: The Latin / Romance Layer (-ate / -ize → -ieren)
latin_ieren.phonetic_rule: English verbs ending in -ate, -ize, -ify, -ish ➔ German verbs ending in -ieren
latin_ieren.historical_linguistics: English verbs derived from Latin or French directly map to German verbs ending in -ieren.
latin_ieren.philological_note: Past participles of -ieren verbs never take the "ge-" prefix (studieren → studiert).
latin_ieren.literature_source: Middle High German productive loan suffix from Old French -ier

strong_verbs_ablaut.name: The 7 Strong Verb Classes (Ablaut)
strong_verbs_ablaut.phonetic_rule: English irregular strong verbs with internal vowel changes ➔ German strong verbs following the exact same Ablautreihe
strong_verbs_ablaut.historical_linguistics: Shared 7 Proto-Germanic verb classes where tenses are formed by shifting root vowels.
